1	# HANDOFF — take over Katalyst and carry it to a working prototype
2	
3	You are a fresh agent. You have no memory of how this project got here. This file gives you everything you need to continue. Read it fully, then read `STATUS.md`, then the plan for the stack you are on.
4	
5	---
6	
7	## 1. The mission
8	
9	Build **Katalyst**: a take-home prototype for Catalyst (catalyst.app), a seed-stage company that turns a trading idea stated in plain English into live execution.
10	
11	**What the tool does, in one sentence:** you type an event you think will happen; Katalyst shows what it would cause, step by step, ending in trades — and lets you change any step to see how the trades change.
12	
13	The brief is `ASSIGNMENT.md`. The owner is **Kent Gang**, a solo developer. He cares most about four things, in his words: well structured with Docker and tests; proper code design; rigorously documented decisions; and a beautiful, elegant, delightful interface.
14	
15	**"Done" means:** a reviewer clones the repo, runs one command, and walks the full flow on all four example events from the brief — type a hypothesis, watch the cause-and-effect map draw itself, change a step, compare the two versions, and end on a thesis card with a derived stop-loss. Tests pass with no API key. Every number on screen can show why. Full checklist: `roadmap-03-to-06.md`, "Definition of done".
16	
17	---
18	
19	## 2. What is built, as of 2026-09-17
20	
21	Stacks 01 (skeleton) and 02 (schema) are **merged to `main`**. Ten pull requests, all squash-merged, `main` green.
22	
23	**Documents.** `PRODUCT_REQUIREMENTS.md` (fourteen invariants, fourteen interface requirements, eleven decisions Kent took in the interview). `ARCHITECTURE.md` (§4, §6, §7, §8 marked *built*; §1, §2, §3, §5 still *planned*). Fourteen decision records in `docs/adr/` — **0001–0014, all accepted**. Read 0014 before touching the engine: it says how a supposition ends and what the range under a computed number means. Six spec chapters written: `spec/graph/{proposition,link,belief,validity}.md` and `spec/multiverse/{interventions,branches-and-worlds}.md`, plus `spec/vocabulary.md` with its **Interface words** table.
24	
25	**The server** — `backend/src/katalyst/`:
26	
27	- `domain/` — the pure core. `belief.py` (`Belief`, `Beliefs`), `proposition.py` (`Proposition`, `Resolution`, `BaseRate`, `Evidence`, `ContractPayoff`, `PricePayoff`), `link.py` (`Link`, `Source`, `Provenance`, `Days`), `graph.py`, `intervention.py` (the six frozen classes and the `Intervention` union), `branch.py`, `ids.py`, `validity.py` (`validate` returning **every** fault at once, twelve violation codes). Everything frozen. Nothing computes yet.
28	- `engine/ids.py` — `mint_id()`, the only place an identifier is made.
29	- `fixtures/hormuz.py` — the worked example: seven claims (`H`, `C`, `B`, `R`, `M1`, `M2`, `N1`), eight arrows, and the branch `br_hormuz_then_strike` with three edits (`Do(H)`, `Insert(S, three arrows)`, `Do(S)`). `fixtures/catalogue.py` lists it.
30	- `api/` — `main.py` mounts everything under `/api/`. Live routes: **`GET /api/healthz`**, **`GET /api/readyz`**, **`GET /api/about`**, **`GET /api/fixtures`**, **`GET /api/fixtures/{id}`**.
31	
32	**The browser app** — `frontend/src/`: `api/schema.ts` (994 lines, generated from the server, never hand-edited), `api/client.ts` (the typed caller), `styles/tokens.css` (the whole visual vocabulary — two themes, three type sizes, three weights, an 8-pixel grid, `--dir-up` / `--dir-down` / `--tail` / `--focus`, contrast ratios written beside every colour), `App.tsx` (one screen reporting three readings).
33	
34	**Tooling.** Docker for development and packaged; `compose.yaml` and `compose.prod.yaml`; a `Makefile` (`dev up down prod test lint types eval`); pre-commit with `commitizen`, `ruff`, `biome`, `gitleaks`; continuous integration with four jobs — `backend`, `frontend`, `types-fresh`, `docker` — **and no API key in any of them**.
35	
36	**Tests: 139 on the server, 3 in the browser app. `domain/` is at 100% coverage.** `mypy --strict` clean on `domain/`. The import-boundary test (`test_domain_imports_nothing_impure`) is green.
37	
38	**Next:** stacks **03a (engine)** and **03b (canvas)**, in parallel — Kent's decision D11. Plans: `stack-03a-engine.md` and `stack-03b-canvas.md`.

42	## 3. Read these, in this order (about 40 minutes)
43	
44	1. `AGENTS.md` — the rules of the repo and the working agreements. **Binding.**
45	2. `PRODUCT_REQUIREMENTS.md` — what and why. §1 (the product in one screen), §3 (eleven decisions Kent already made — do not reopen them), §7 (the interface requirements, UX-1 to UX-14), §9 (fourteen invariants), §10 (anti-patterns), §12 (the roadmap as stacks of pull requests).
46	3. `ARCHITECTURE.md` — how it is built. Every section is marked *planned* or *built*. **You must update it in the same pull request that makes a section real.**
47	4. `spec/README.md` and `spec/vocabulary.md` — the spec is a book, one directory per idea. Use the vocabulary's words exactly, in code, docs, and interface text. The **Interface words** table is the only source for button and badge wording.
48	5. `docs/adr/README.md`, then the decision records your stack depends on (each plan file lists them).
49	6. Skim `docs/research/` only when a plan points you there. The reports are inputs, not decisions — and Kent has rejected one of their recommendations (research report 03's "Instrument" minimalism; the look is the Workbench, decision D3).
50	
51	---
52	
53	## 4. How Kent works — the rules that will get your work rejected if you break them
54	
55	**Build aggressively through milestones.** Kent's own words: *"build aggressively through milestones, I edit after the fact."* He is a co-developer, not an approver standing at a gate. Decision records and spec chapters still come first in the *stack order* — the bottom pull request of every stack is docs-only — but code above them proceeds while he reads. Nothing here is irreversible.
56	
57	**Push and open pull requests freely. Kent merges** — or asks the coordinator to merge, in which case use the method in §5. Never merge without being asked.
58	
59	**All sub-agents run on Opus.** Kent said so directly. Do not downgrade a sub-agent to save tokens.
60	
61	**Decisions come before code.** A significant architectural choice needs a decision record (`docs/adr/`, next number is `0015`, copy `template.md`). Write it with status `proposed`, ask Kent, and build only after he accepts. Records 0001–0011 and 0013 are accepted; **0012 (replay mode) is still proposed — build nothing against it.** Small tooling choices already covered by a record need no new one.
62	
63	**Two things Kent will veto on sight.**
64	1. **A template-looking interface.** Default component-library styling, a spinner followed by a dump of results, pop-up dialogs, a tangled hairball graph. Every visual must be deliberately ours.
65	2. **Not knowing why it did that.** Any state that cannot be traced to an input, a rule, or a cited source. This applies to the product *and* to your own work: explain what you did and why, leave a trail.
66	
67	**Write plainly.** Docs, code comments, docstrings, and interface text: no unexplained jargon, abbreviations, or symbols; each passage stands alone; short and punchy. Kent rewrote early drafts for being obtuse. When you cite an invariant such as INV-4, add a few words saying what it means.
68	
69	**The spec is a book; decision records are a journal.** Spec files are named by idea and live in the directory for that idea. Do not number spec files. Decision records are numbered because they happen in order.
70	
71	**Authority stays with Kent.** Offer options with a recommendation; do not argue him into things. When he decides, record it and move on. Questions for him go at the bottom of `STATUS.md` under "Waiting on Kent", one line each, with the date — **and in chat**, because he does not read `plans/` unprompted.
72	
73	---
74	
75	## 5. Git and pull requests (decision record 0009)
76	
77	- **Branch names:** `<type>/<NN>-<slug>`, where `NN` is the stack number — `feat/03a-apply`, `spec/03b-workbench`.
78	- **Commit messages:** Conventional Commits — `feat:`, `fix:`, `refactor:`, `test:`, `docs:`, `chore:`, plus two local types, `spec:` and `adr:`. End agent-written commits with the co-author line your session instructions give you.
79	- **Stacks:** the bottom pull request targets `main`; each one above targets its parent branch — `gh pr create --base <parent-branch>`. At most four deep.
80	- **Pull request body, three headings:** *What* · *Which invariant it satisfies* · *What is deliberately not here*. End with the generated-with line your session instructions give you.
81	- **Merging:** squash, keeping the conventional prefix in the subject. `main` stays green.
82	- **Never commit or push to `main` directly.** Never force-push a branch Kent is reviewing without telling him.
83	
84	### Merging a stack — the method that actually works
85	
86	**`gh pr merge` refuses a stacked pull request.** It errors out because the head branch is not based on the default branch. Use the merge-queue API directly, bottom pull request first:
87	
88	```bash
89	gh api -X PUT repos/kgang/katalyst/pulls/<n>/merge-async \
90	  -f merge_method=squash \
91	  -f commit_title="<subject> (#<n>)" \
92	  -f commit_message="<the What section of the body>" \
93	  -f sha=<head sha of that branch>
94	```
95	
96	It answers with a job identifier. Poll it until it reports done:
97	
98	```bash
99	gh api repos/kgang/katalyst/pulls/<n>/merge-async/<uuid>
100	```
101	
102	Then move up the stack. Three rules that will save you an hour:
103	
104	1. **Bottom-up, always.** Merge the pull request whose base is `main` first. Merging the top of a stack with `gh pr merge` merges it **into its parent branch**, not into `main` — it looks like it worked and it silently did the wrong thing. Never do it.
105	2. **A child branch that already merged in a sibling stack needs `git merge origin/main` first**, then a push, before its own merge will go through cleanly. This happens whenever two stacks ran in parallel and touched the same file.
106	3. **Delete the branches afterwards** (`gh api -X DELETE repos/kgang/katalyst/git/refs/heads/<branch>`, or the `--delete-branch` flag on the next `gh pr merge` that does work), and remove the worktrees with `git worktree remove`.
107	
108	---
109	
110	## 6. Your environment (checked 2026-09-17)
111	
112	| Tool | Version here | Note |
113	|------|--------------|------|
114	| `gh` (GitHub command line) | 2.101.0, signed in as `kgang` | Repo is `kgang/katalyst`, private. No stack commands exist in `gh`; use `--base`, and §5's method to merge |
115	| `uv` (Python package manager) | 0.12.15 | Current |
116	| Python | 3.12.4 | Matches decision record 0002 |
117	| Node | 23.3.0 locally — an odd, short-lived release | Fine locally. Docker and continuous integration pin **24** (long-term support) |
118	| Docker | 27.5.1 | Supports `docker compose watch` |
119	| `jq` | 1.8.1 | |
120	
121	**`.env` in the main checkout is Kent's.** It is git-ignored and it holds his real keys. **Never copy it into a worktree, never read it into a brief, never commit it.** A previous session created a stray copy in a Docker worktree and had to remove it. `.env.example` is the one agents use.
122	
123	**Hooks:** `.claude/settings.json` runs the `entire` command-line tool on session events. It pushes checkpoint refs on `git push`; that output is normal.
124	
125	**Model API key:** not needed until stack 04. Before writing *any* code that calls Claude, load the `claude-api` skill — model names and request shapes changed recently, and memory is unreliable. Decision record 0006 holds the verified specifics.
126	
127	---
128	
129	## 7. The worktree pattern
130	
131	Every sub-agent gets its own checkout of its own branch under **`../katalyst-wt/<branch-slug>/`**. The main checkout stays on `main` and is never used by a sub-agent.
132	
133	```bash
134	git worktree add ../katalyst-wt/feat-03a-apply -b feat/03a-apply <base-branch>
135	```
136	
137	The rules, and they are not negotiable because they are what keeps eight parallel agents from stepping on each other:
138	
139	- **One agent per worktree**, except for chapter writers, who may share one worktree **only** when their files are disjoint and **none of them runs a git command**.
140	- **Disjoint owned files.** Every brief carries an explicit list. "Touch nothing outside it. If you believe something outside it must change, write why in your report and stop."
141	- **Agents never push, never open a pull request, never touch `main`.** They commit on their branch and report. The coordinator reviews, then pushes and opens the pull request.
142	- **Remove worktrees after the merge:** `git worktree remove ../katalyst-wt/<slug>`.
143	
144	---
145	
146	## 8. Lessons — read these twice
147	
148	1. **After any interruption, check reality before acting.** Run `git log --oneline -5`, `git status`, `gh pr list`, and read `STATUS.md`. A previous agent lost part of its context mid-session and re-did work that was already committed — overwrote a committed file and launched sub-agents to revise approved text. It was caught and reverted, but only by luck. Do not trust your memory of the repo; trust the repo.
149	2. **Append to `STATUS.md` before you stop**, every time. It is how the next agent — or you, after a context loss — finds the thread.
150	3. **Brief sub-agents fully.** They know only what you tell them. Give each a disjoint set of files. Paste the pre-decisions, never link them: `plans/` is git-ignored and the agent may be in a worktree that cannot see it.
151	4. **Keep cross-references consistent.** One rename touched 26 references across 12 files. After any rename, search the whole repo for the old name.
152	5. **Status lives in three places** for a decision record: its own front-matter, `docs/adr/README.md`, and the table in `ARCHITECTURE.md` §9. Change all three together.
153	6. **Verify every sub-agent's claim yourself.** Run the tests, run the lints, read the diff, look at the screen. Agents flagged real inconsistencies last session and also drifted once (`retune` used for the wrong thing). A report is a hypothesis, not evidence.
154	7. **Write the shapes sheet before the parallel writers start.** The stack 02 shapes sheet is why six chapters and two code agents used the same field names. Without it you get six different answers to the same small question, and the reconciliation costs more than the sheet did.
155	8. **Put a reviewer agent over parallel writers.** The read-only reviewer over the six stack-02 chapters found five blocking problems and about twenty consistency ones before Kent saw a word. It is the cheapest agent you will run.
156	9. **Sub-agents sometimes write the wrong co-author line.** Harmless: every pull request is squash-merged, and the coordinator writes the squash message. Do not spend time correcting it on the branch.
157	10. **The first pull request of a stack is usually small enough to write yourself.** Stack 01's README took twenty minutes of coordinator time and unblocked the next agent immediately. Launching a sub-agent for it would have cost more in briefing than in typing. The same trick works for chapter *stubs*: commit the headings, and the code agent can branch off the spec branch before the chapters are written.
158	
159	---
160	
161	## 9. The road from here
162	
163	| Stack | What it proves | Plan |
164	|-------|----------------|------|
165	| ~~01 skeleton~~ | **Merged.** Both halves say hello; Docker, continuous integration, pre-commit; types flow from server to browser | `stack-01-skeleton.md` (history) |
166	| ~~02 schema~~ | **Merged.** The data shapes exist, reject bad graphs, and the Hormuz example loads end to end | `stack-02-schema.md` (history) |
167	| **03a engine ∥ 03b canvas** | **Next.** Changing one step re-computes only what is downstream; the map is beautiful and readable | `stack-03a-engine.md`, `stack-03b-canvas.md` |
168	| 04 generation | The model draws a real map for any hypothesis, streamed step by step; replay mode if record 0012 is accepted | `roadmap-03-to-06.md` |
169	| 05 thesis | The map compiles to a trade with a derived stop-loss and live market prices | `roadmap-03-to-06.md` |
170	| 06 probes | Extra modeling effort where the user points it (stretch) | `roadmap-03-to-06.md` |
171	
172	Stacks 03a and 03b run in parallel — Kent chose this (D11). Everything else is sequential. The two stacks touch disjoint files except `frontend/src/api/schema.ts` (03a's, this cycle) and `ARCHITECTURE.md` (split by section); both plans say how.
173	
174	**Start with `stack-03a-engine.md` and `stack-03b-canvas.md`, together.**

76	`apply` folds a branch's edits onto a map, in order, and hands back the map it leaves behind together with every value an edit fixed. It is pure: no clock, no network, no randomness. The optional third argument is what makes law 2 type-check — feed back what a previous `apply` returned and you can apply the next branch on top:

82	**What each edit does to the map.** `do`: remove every arrow whose target is this claim **and that is present right now** — a timed assertion, not a seal — and record an assignment. `observe`: remove nothing; record an assignment. `insert`: add the claim and its arrows. `retune`: replace one arrow's `strength` and nothing else. `believe`: write `beliefs.user` on one claim and nothing else, anywhere. `refine`: **not implemented** — return a violation saying it arrives in stack 06.

So `flatten(branches: Mapping[BranchId, Branch], branch_id: BranchId) -> tuple[Intervention, ...]` walks the parent chain and concatenates. A parent chain that loops back on itself returns a violation rather than hanging (`branches-and-worlds.md` open question 3, answered here for the walk only — the storage rule is still stack 05's).

114	## Pull request 3 — `propagate`
115	
116	```python
117	def propagate(
118	    graph: Graph,
119	    assignments: tuple[Assignment, ...],
120	    *,
121	    as_of: date,
122	    seed: int,
123	    versions: int = 2_000,   # the outer loop: versions of the map (how sure we are of the inputs)
124	    worlds: int = 8,         # the inner loop: worlds per version (how the dice fall)
125	) -> World
126	```
127	
128	Sixteen thousand worlds in total, and the two numbers are not interchangeable — they measure two different kinds of not-knowing. The next three sections say which is which and why the split is 2 000 × 8 rather than 10 000 × 1. Measured cost: about **ten milliseconds at sixty claims**.
129	
130	### The time axis
131	
132	Day zero is `as_of`. The window runs from day zero to the latest resolve-by date on the map, in whole days. Every date becomes an integer day index at the edge of this function and stays an integer inside it.
133	
134	**When a claim is settled, which is not the same as whether it is true.** Every claim gets a day on which it is settled — the day its clock starts, so that any arrow leaving it measures elapsed days from there. If an assignment fixes it, that day is the assignment's `at` (day zero when `at` is `None`). Otherwise it is the earliest day any live incoming arrow reaches it: the day that arrow's source was settled, plus the arrow's `lag`. A claim with neither an assignment nor a live incoming arrow is settled on **day zero** — the map carries no timing information about it, so its clock starts at the beginning of the window.
135	
136	**Being settled says nothing about being true.** A claim with no assignment is sampled from its own `prior`, every draw, exactly as always; nothing is ever forced true because its clock started. The two ideas are separate and conflating them is the mistake this paragraph exists to prevent. It follows that `t_source` — when each claim was settled — is a **schedule computed once from the shape of the map**, the same in every draw, while **truth is per draw**: an arrow's term is non-zero only in those draws where its source came out true. One schedule, sixteen thousand different worlds running along it.
137	
138	### The arithmetic
139	
140	At day *t*, for each claim, in an order that always puts causes before effects (topological, reflexive arrows set aside):
141	
142	```
143	log-odds(claim, t) = baseline(claim, t) + Σ over live incoming arrows: strength × shape(t − t_source)
144	```
145	
146	`shape` is a plain function of elapsed days, zero before it: `impulse` — zero through the lag, then 1, halving every `half_life` day thereafter; `step` — zero through the lag, then 1, held; `ramp` — climbing from 0 to 1 across the lag, then 1, held. A `sustain` arrow's term is zero on any day its source is not true; a `trigger` arrow's term keeps running on its own schedule once fired, whatever the source does afterwards. **That one sentence is the whole domino-and-apple distinction as arithmetic.** Write it in the chapter with the two ASCII pictures `link.md` already draws.
147	
148	`baseline(claim, t)` is the log-odds of the claim's own `prior`. A supposition is **not** a baseline term — see the next section; while it holds, the claim's value is not computed at all.
149	
150	### How a supposition ends — **Kent, 2026-09-17**
151	
152	**A supposition is a hard fact until something undermines it.** While a `do` holds, the claim is simply **true in every draw** — not a large log-odds baseline that arrows can argue with. There is no ±4.0, no .98, no number at all: the tile shows the word *Supposed* and its date where a likelihood would go. That is what "suppose this is true" means in English, and a tool that answered "suppose this is true" with `.98` would be lying about what the user asked for.
153	
154	**It stops holding on the day the *cause* of the first live opposing arrow becomes true.** Not the day that arrow's push reaches full size — the day the world changed. In code: `Retraction.at = t_source`, and the arrow's own `lag` then does its ordinary work afterwards. From that day the claim is computed like any other: its own prior, plus every live arrow, each arriving on its own schedule.
155	
156	On the Hormuz strike branch, with day zero at 2026-10-01:
157	
158	| Days | What `H` reads | Why |
159	|---|---|---|
160	| Oct 1 | **Supposed · Oct 1** — a word, not a number | The `do` holds; `H` is true in every draw |
161	| Oct 2 – Oct 4 | **.35**, the series marked *withdrawn — no live push yet* | `S` became true on Oct 2, so the supposition is withdrawn that day. `S -> H` carries `lag=3`, so nothing is pushing yet and `H` falls back to its own prior |
162	| Oct 5 onward | **about .07**, the series marked *pushed* | `S -> H`'s step reaches full size and pushes `H` down |

164	The tile reads *Supposed · Oct 1 → Retracted · Oct 2 · by "a confirmed military strike on Iranian territory"* — UX-14 word for word — and the three-day gap between the date on the badge and the day the number moves is not a bug to hide. It is the honest shape of the answer, and the series has to be able to say so, which is why every day of a claim's series carries a named state:
165	
166	```python
167	SeriesState = Literal["sampled", "supposed", "withdrawn", "pushed"]
168	# sampled   — the ordinary case: no supposition has ever touched this claim
169	# supposed  — a `do` is holding; the claim is true in every draw and the tile shows a word
170	# withdrawn — the supposition has been undermined and no opposing push has arrived yet
171	# pushed    — an opposing push is live
172	```

176	    target: PropositionId    # the claim whose supposition ended
177	    at: date                 # the day it ended — the day the opposing arrow's SOURCE became true

185	### Randomness, and the two seed streams
186	
187	Everything comes from the one `seed` argument, through `numpy.random.Generator` objects built from it and nothing else. No module-level generator, no clock, no global state, ever. The same `(map, branch, seed)` gives byte-identical worlds on any machine — NFR-2, pinned by `test_world_replays_from_base_branch_seed`.
188	
189	There are **two streams**, and keeping them apart is load-bearing:
190	
191	| Stream | Drives | Rule |
192	|---|---|---|
193	| `params` | The outer loop — which 2 000 versions of the map we try | **Must not depend on the branch.** A base world and a branch world built from the same seed use the *same* 2 000 versions |
194	| `worlds` | The inner loop — how the dice fall inside one version | Ordinary; may depend on anything |
195	
196	The `params` rule is what makes a difference between two worlds readable. Compare a base world and a branch world version by version and the only thing that changed is the edit — the numbers underneath were held fixed. That is *common random numbers*, and without it every comparison is the user's change plus a wash of sampling noise, which is exactly the failure `branches-and-worlds.md` anti-pattern 4 describes. `test_same_seed_same_world` covers both streams.
197	
198	`observe` is handled in the **inner** loop: inside each version, keep only the worlds in which the claim came out as observed, then weight that version by its survival share when the two loops are pooled. Five lines of importance weighting. When survival is low the world carries a loud warning — and the warning says the **range** is unreliable, not just the point, because a version that survived twice out of eight is contributing a very noisy number to the band.
199	
200	### The range on a computed belief — **Kent, 2026-09-17** (decision record 0014)
201	
202	**Two kinds of not-knowing, and the whole design is keeping them apart.**
203	
204	- **How the dice fall.** The strait either opens or it does not. That is already inside `p`: `p` is the share of worlds in which the claim came out true.
205	- **How sure we are of the numbers we put in.** Every prior on the map was elicited, and a different but equally defensible set of priors would give a different `p`. **That** is the range.
206	
207	So a wide band means *"we are not sure what number to give you; more homework would move it"* — never *"the event is more volatile"*. That is the one sentence a trader has to be able to repeat, and the chip label says it: **model interval, uncalibrated · how sure we are of `.35` — not how much the world can move.** The formal name is a second-order, or two-dimensional, Monte Carlo; the literature is in the research note.
208	
209	**What a stated `{p, lo, hi}` means: a split logit-normal.** `p` is the median. `lo` and `hi` are the 10th and 90th percentiles — "eight times in ten". The two halves are fitted separately on the log-odds scale:
210	
211	```
212	s_lo = (logit(p) − logit(lo)) / 1.2816        # 1.2816 is the 90th percentile of a standard normal
213	s_hi = (logit(hi) − logit(p)) / 1.2816
214	```
215	
216	Separately, because real elicited ranges are lopsided: the fixture's own ranges are near-symmetric on log-odds (mean gap ratio 0.94) and clearly skewed on probability (1.26). This shape honours all three stated numbers exactly, stays inside 0 and 1 with no clamping, and needs no new fields on `Belief`. One consequence to write in the chapter rather than let a reader trip over: the mean of a split logit-normal sits slightly above its median when `p < .5`, so a claim's `prior.p` and its computed `beliefs.model.p` differ by a hair even for the hypothesis, which has no causes (H: `.35` → `.36`).
217	
218	**The loop.**
219	
220	1. Draw **2 000 versions** of the map with a Latin hypercube over every prior's fitted shape — numpy only, three lines; `scipy` is not worth a dependency for this.
221	2. Inside each version, run **8 worlds**.
222	3. **Rao-Blackwellise the last step**: for each claim keep the *probability* it came out true in that world, not only the coin flip. Free variance reduction — the number is already computed.
223	4. **Correct for inner noise** with the law of total variance, so that what is left is the spread across versions and not the spread across eight coin flips:
224	
225	```
226	f = sqrt(max(0, 1 − mean(inner_var / worlds) / var(q)))
227	q_corrected = mean(q) + (q − mean(q)) · f
228	```
229	
230	5. `p` is the mean over both loops. `lo` and `hi` are the 10th and 90th percentiles of the corrected version-level values.
231	
232	**Measured, on Hormuz claim B at day 45, against the exact answer by enumeration — `.35 (.20–.49)`:**
233	
234	| Design | Reports | Wobble of the band edges across seeds |
235	|---|---|---|
236	| Three runs: all lows, then all highs | `.19–.50`, and it is not a bound — `R → B` is negative, so the true corner is `.158–.567` | none |
237	| 20 batches of 500 | `.25–.46` — a quarter of that width is coin-flip noise, and the band is 28% too narrow | ±.021 |
238	| The analytic delta method | `.22–.52`, accurate to .004, but fifty times slower and first-order only | none |
239	| **2 000 × 8, Rao-Blackwellised, noise-corrected** | **`.20–.50`** | **±.002 to ±.003**, about 10 ms at 60 claims |
240	
241	The delta method is kept — not as the engine, but as a **cross-check in a test**.
242	
243	**Link strengths are fixed in 03a**, and the chapter says so plainly: only priors vary between versions. There is no `strength_lo` and no `strength_hi`, now or ever — widening an arrow is derived from its `provenance` ("how well-backed" becomes "how wide") and that ships in **stack 04**, where arrows finally differ from one another. Every arrow in today's fixture is hand-written `argued` or `asserted`, so doing it now would widen everything by the same amount and teach nobody anything.
244	
245	**FR-21 falls out for free.** From the same outer sample, a bin estimator gives each claim's **first-order share of another claim's band** — six lines of numpy. On the fixture, 92% of B's band is B's own prior; pin that down and the band goes from 29 points to 8, while everything else contributes less than half a point. That is a better answer than "sensitivity × width" and it is the number FR-21's "where to spend modeling budget" ranking becomes. It is carried on the world as
246	
247	```python
248	range_shares: Mapping[PropositionId, Mapping[PropositionId, float]]
249	# range_shares[target][source] = the share of target's band explained by source's prior
250	```
251	
252	and **no route reads it until stack 06.** It is computed and carried now because the sample it comes from is thrown away otherwise.

254	**Two things the chapter must warn about**, both measured and both counter-intuitive:
255	
256	- **A `do` does not reliably narrow what is downstream.** It collapses the target's own band, but B's width went *up* under `do(H)` — `.292` to `.323` — because the logistic curve is steeper near `.45`. The honest thing to show is the share, not the width: H's contribution to B's band went from 2.6% to 0%.

260	
261	```python
262	class World(BaseModel):                                   # frozen
263	    base_id: str
264	    branch_id: BranchId | None
265	    seed: int
266	    versions: int                                         # the outer loop — how sure we are of the inputs
267	    worlds: int                                           # the inner loop — how the dice fall

282	`series` is what makes UX-3's scrubbable time axis possible, and `states` is what lets the canvas say *Supposed* where a number would be misleading and *withdrawn — no live push yet* where a number would be confusing. Cap the series: if the window is longer than 180 days, sample it to 180 points and say so in `warnings`.
283	
284	**`conditionals` means *supposed*, not *observed*, and it is computed lazily.** The number on a wire's midpoint chip is the target's likelihood **with that arrow's source supposed true** — a `do`, the interventional number. It is never the observed number: "how often do these two show up together" is exactly the correlational quantity `link.md`'s anti-pattern 3 refuses, and putting it on a wire that claims a mechanism would be the worst kind of quiet lie.

286	Computing it costs a whole extra propagation per arrow — eight on the Hormuz map, about eighty on a sixty-claim one, so more than a tenfold increase on every world build for a number most users never open. So **compute it lazily**: `World.conditionals` is empty when a world is built, and `POST /api/worlds/conditional` (base, branch, seed, one link identifier) returns the one number when something asks. Laziness costs nothing in honesty here, because the number is still a pure function of the same three inputs plus the arrow — the same seed gives the same answer whenever it is asked, so a lazily fetched number is byte-identical to an eagerly computed one.

328	**3. No computed number is ever typed by hand.** The fixture's hand-written `beliefs.model` values go. The clean version — and this is the recommendation to implement unless Kent says otherwise — is that **`beliefs.model` in the fixture becomes equal to `prior`**, which is the truthful statement "nothing has been computed yet", and the served bundle carries the engine's world beside the map once the world route exists. 332	## Pull request 4 — difference, sensitivity, and the routes
333	
334	**`diff(world_a, world_b) -> Diff`.** Per claim, one of four states:
335	
336	| State | When |
337	|---|---|
338	| `unchanged` | Present in both, and it fails either half of the `shifted` test below |
339	| `shifted` | Present in both, it moved by **0.005 or more**, **and** it moved the *same way* in at least **90% of the 2 000 versions**. Carries before, after, the signed difference, and that share |
340	| `added` | Present in B and not in A |
341	| `killed` | Present in both, and in B it is either assigned false or no longer has any path from the hypothesis. *Never* "its number got small" — the vocabulary says `killed` means forced false or cut off |
342	
343	**How `shifted` is decided — read it off the paired difference, never off band overlap** (Kent, 2026-09-17). Because the `params` seed stream does not depend on the branch, version *k* of the base world and version *k* of the branch world were built from the *same* underlying numbers. Subtract them version by version and what is left is the edit, with the elicitation noise cancelled out — common random numbers. Comparing the two bands instead would be badly wrong, and the fixture shows exactly how: under `do(H)`, B's two bands **overlap by a third**, and yet **100% of versions move the same way** (+.10, with a 10-to-90 band of +.07 to +.13). Band overlap would report "no change" about the single clearest change on the map.
344	
345	That share of versions agreeing on the direction is called **agreement** — the vocabulary's reserved word for a number computed from how far independent runs differed, never self-reported — and it is a column on the row beside `range_width`.
346	
347	Plus **ranked terminal deltas** — every `market` and `not_tradeable` claim that shifted. **Two factors, and only two** (Kent, 2026-09-17):
348	
349	```
350	rank = |Δ likelihood|  ×  min(provenance weight of each arrow on the shortest path
351	                              from the edit's subject to this terminal)
352	```
353	
354	with provenance weights `documented` 1.0 · `historical` 0.9 · `market_implied` 0.9 · `argued` 0.6 · `user` 0.6 · `simulated` 0.5 · `asserted` 0.3. That is FR-16's "size of the change and how well-founded it is", made arithmetic: how big, times how much the weakest arrow behind it is worth.
355	
356	**Range width is data, not a factor.** `DeltaRow` carries `range_width` so the delta rail can show it as **its own column**, and nothing multiplies it into the rank. Folding width into the score buries two different facts inside one number — "this moved a lot" and "we are unsure how much" are separate things a trader weighs separately, and a single blended score hides which one is talking.
357	
358	**Which day a number is read on** (Kent, 2026-09-17), because the two surfaces want different days:
359	
360	| Surface | Day | Why |
361	|---|---|---|
362	| A tile's headline belief | The claim's own **resolve-by day** | INV-1 guarantees every claim has one, and it is the day the claim is judged. The number on the tile is therefore the number the tile's own date refers to |
363	| A delta rail row | The **day of largest divergence** between the two worlds | A change that shows up for a fortnight and then unwinds is the thing a trader acts on, and reading it on a distant resolve-by day would show nothing. The row carries `at_day` and `peak_delta`, and names the date on screen |
364	
365	```python
366	class DeltaRow(BaseModel):
367	    target: PropositionId
368	    before: float          # at at_day
369	    after: float           # at at_day
370	    peak_delta: float      # signed; the largest divergence over the window
371	    at_day: date           # the day that divergence is largest
372	    range_width: float     # a column in the delta rail; never multiplied into rank
373	    agreement: float       # share of versions that moved the same way; a column, never a factor
374	    rank: float            # |peak_delta| × weakest provenance weight on the path. Two factors
375	```
376	
377	`range_width` and `agreement` are both **columns and never factors**. They answer different questions — *how unsure are we of this number* and *how sure are we of its direction* — and a trader weighs them separately. Folding either into one score hides which of the three things is talking.
378	
379	**A known wart, written down rather than hidden.** INV-8's path product multiplies likelihoods that were each read on their own resolve-by day, so it multiplies numbers from different days. It is defensible — each factor is the number that claim will be judged on — but it is not a joint likelihood at a single instant, and `diff.md` must say so in one sentence rather than letting a reader assume otherwise.
380	
381	Plus a **one-line summary** built from a fixed template, never free prose: *"<edit in the user's words> moves <terminal> from <before> to <after> by <date> and leaves <n> claims untouched."*
382	
383	**`sensitivity(world) -> tuple[SensitivityRow, ...]`.** Flip each claim one at a time — a `do` to the opposite of whichever way it more often comes out — re-propagate, and record the signed difference on every terminal. A sweep is one re-propagation per claim, so it runs at a **reduced budget — 250 versions × 8 worlds, about 2 000 worlds per flip** rather than the full 16 000 — and every row says which budget produced it. This feeds stack 05's derived stop-loss and stack 06's "spend here" ranking; **no route in this stack**, because nothing on screen reads it yet.
384	
385	**The routes**, in `backend/src/katalyst/api/worlds.py`, under the `/api/` prefix like everything else:
386	
387	| Route | Body | Answer |
388	|---|---|---|
389	| `POST /api/worlds` | `{base_id, branch, seed, versions?, worlds?}` — `branch` is a whole `Branch`, sent by the browser, not a stored identifier (there is no store until stack 05) | One `World` |
390	| `POST /api/worlds/diff` | `{base_id, branch_a, branch_b, seed, versions?, worlds?}` — both worlds are built with the **same** `params` stream, which is what makes the paired difference meaningful | One `Diff` |
391	| `POST /api/worlds/conditional` | `{base_id, branch, seed, link_id}` | One `Belief`: the target's likelihood with that arrow's source **supposed** true. Lazy, one arrow at a time — see pull request 3 |
392	
393	`engine/worlds.py` sits between the route and `domain/`: it finds the base map in `fixtures.catalogue`, resolves the parent chain with `flatten`, reads `as_of` from the stored example's `fixture_date`, mints identifiers, and passes a seed through. It is the only place any of that happens, because `domain/` reads no clock and knows no store.
394	
395	A rejected edit comes back as **422 with the list of violations**, each with its code, its subject and its plain sentence — the same shape a rejected proposal already has. Never a 500, never a silent repair.
396	
397	Then: run `make types`, read the generated `frontend/src/api/schema.ts` end to end, and fix the pydantic side if a union reads badly. Never hand-patch the generated file. Finally mark `ARCHITECTURE.md` §3 (the flow of a generation — steps 4 and 7 are now real), §5 (where each invariant is enforced) and §10 (its open question about a deterministic sweep is answered) with what is true.

76	
77	Stack 03a is building the world route at the same time as this stack. The seam that keeps them apart:
78	
79	```ts
80	export interface WorldSource {
81	  /** The base map and its branches, as the fixture route already serves them. */
82	  readBundle(id: string): Promise<FixtureBundle>;
83	  /** One world. Its numbers are OPTIONAL — see below. */
84	  readWorld(request: WorldRequest): Promise<WorldView>;
85	}
86	```
87	
88	Two implementations. `FixtureWorldSource` reads `GET /api/fixtures/hormuz` and uses the fixture's stored `beliefs.model` for the base world — honest, because the fixture says in its own comments that those are illustrative. `ApiWorldSource` calls `POST /api/worlds` and `POST /api/worlds/diff`.
89	
90	**And for the second world, before the engine exists, there is no second set of numbers at all** (Kent, 2026-09-17). No committed illustrative file, no hand-written likelihoods, no "illustrative numbers" chip. Numbers nobody computed are exactly the state a user cannot trace, and a plan that ships them for one stack ships them.
91	
92	**What the diff view shows instead is structure, and structure is real.** It is computed from the branch — which this stack already has, because the fixture serves it — and it needs no arithmetic whatsoever:
93	
94	| State | Computed from the branch by |
95	|---|---|
96	| `added` | The claim arrives in an `insert` |
97	| `killed` | The claim is the target of a `do(…, false)`, or the edits leave it with no path from the hypothesis |
98	| `downstream` | The claim is in the affected set of at least one edit — it is a claim your change can move |
99	| `untouched` | Everything else. Byte-identical, and the canvas can say so with confidence |
100	
101	That is a genuinely useful view on its own: *"here is what your edit can reach, and here is what it provably cannot"* is the product's central correctness claim made visible, and it is the half of the diff that does not depend on the engine at all. Following arrows is **reachability, not arithmetic** — no strength is added, no likelihood is moved — so it does not break this stack's rule. When 03a lands, the server's `affected_set` is the authority and the browser's version becomes a hint that must agree with it; a component test pins the two against the Hormuz branch.
102	
103	So every number slot in `WorldView` is optional, and an absent number **renders as an absence with a reason** — *"no engine yet"* in this stack, *"no market"* for an unpriced claim, a dash inviting your own number for an empty user slot. 111	## Pull request 3 — wires, the colour law, the Inspector
112	
113	**Wires are custom edges**, drawn with `getSmoothStepPath` and a midpoint chip through `EdgeLabelRenderer`. **The stroke says one thing and one thing only: what kind of push this is** (Kent, 2026-09-17). Five encodings, each readable without colour:
114	
115	| What | How |
116	|---|---|
117	| Signal shape | Stroke pattern: `impulse` dot-dash · `step` solid · `ramp` a gradient along the stroke |
118	| Strength | Stroke width, from `|strength|`, regardless of sign. Four steps, not a continuous ramp |
119	| `sustain` versus `trigger` | A `sustain` wire is double-stroked. A `trigger` wire is single |
120	| `reflexive` | The wire loops back on itself and carries a **lag chip** reading the delay in days |
121	| Provenance | **An origin mark at the wire's tail**, where the arrow leaves its cause — not the stroke. Three steps: **●●●** `documented`, `historical`, `market_implied` · **●●** `argued`, `user` · **●** `asserted`, `simulated`. The exact word is in the Inspector |
122	
123	**Why provenance left the stroke.** One channel cannot carry two meanings. The stroke already says `impulse` or `step` or `ramp`, and stack 02 gave it that job; asking it to also say `argued` or `documented` means a dot-dash-and-dashed wire that says neither clearly. A three-step mark at the tail says the useful thing at a glance — *is there a document behind this, or is it the model talking* — and the seven-way distinction, which nobody reads off a picture anyway, lives in the Inspector where there is room for the word. Build it as one small component, `OriginMark`, used by the wire and by the Inspector so the two can never disagree. INV-12 still holds: provenance is visible on every wire and no hue is involved.
124	
125	**The midpoint chip** shows the conditional likelihood in the arrow-and-bar idiom the forecasting site Metaculus uses: the target's likelihood **with this arrow's source supposed true**. That number is **not computed here** and it is **not on the world** — stack 03a computes it lazily, one arrow at a time, through `POST /api/worlds/conditional`, because computing all of them costs a whole extra propagation per arrow. So the canvas asks for it when a wire is hovered or selected and caches the answer. Until it has one — and always, in this stack, since the route does not exist yet — the chip shows the arrow's push read back in words, *"+1.6 · a strong push toward"*, which is data already on the link and needs no arithmetic. **Never a guessed number.**
126	
127	**The colour law**, in one place, as CSS custom properties added to `frontend/src/styles/tokens.css` under a clearly marked new block. No existing token changes value.
128	
129	| Axis | Channel | Tokens |
130	|---|---|---|
131	| Likelihood | Brightness — a five-step luminance ramp | `--p-0` … `--p-4`, each with its contrast ratio in a comment, as every existing token has |
132	| Direction of financial effect | Hue **plus a glyph plus a sign**, never hue alone | `--dir-up` (blue, ▲) and `--dir-down` (amber, ▼), both already in `tokens.css` |
133	| Tail risk | Texture | `--tail`, the hatch already in `tokens.css` |
134	| The kind of push | Stroke pattern, width and doubling | `impulse` dot-dash · `step` solid · `ramp` gradient; width from `|strength|`; `sustain` doubled |
135	| Provenance | **A mark, not a stroke** | The three-step origin mark at the wire's tail, above (Kent, 2026-09-17) |
136	| Branch identity | Its own small palette, on lanes and chips only — never on a tile's meaning | Violet, teal, rose, slate (*decided here*, accepted 2026-09-17). **Not amber**: amber already means "downward", and one hue cannot mean two things |
137	
138	**The hover lens.** Hovering a tile dims everything not on its ancestor-or-descendant path to 15%. The research calls this the single highest-value interaction for legibility, and it is four lines of state.
139	
140	**The Inspector is a persistent side panel and there are no pop-ups** (UX-10). It shows, for a claim: the full text, the resolution criteria and adjudicating source, the resolve-by date, the base rate with its reference class and its `k` of `n`, all three beliefs with owners, the evidence list, and — when the world carries one — the decomposition that makes the number explicable: *prior, then one line per incoming arrow with its push and its reason, then the result.* `spec/graph/belief.md` §B4 draws that block; copy its layout. **Reserve a slot directly under the range for "why is this band wide?"** — the answer is one sentence naming the claim whose own prior explains most of it (*"92% of this band is B's own starting number; pin that down and the band goes from 29 points to 8"*), it is computed from `World.range_shares`, and **it ships in stack 06, not here.** Leave the slot, leave a comment naming `range_shares`, render nothing. For an arrow: the rationale, the strength read back in words ("+1.6 — a strong push toward"), the mode in words, the lag, the shape, the sources with the day each was fetched, and the provenance in full — the word, with the same `OriginMark` the wire draws, so the mark and the word are one component and cannot drift apart.
141	
142	**The path-product bar (INV-8).** Select a claim and a bar shows the multiplied-out likelihood of the path from the hypothesis to it, beside the story sentence. The product arrives on the world; this stack renders it. If it is absent, the bar says "no path shown" — it never multiplies anything itself.

146	## Pull request 4 — two worlds, the branch panel, the keyboard
147	
148	**The ghost overlay.** Lay out the union of both worlds **once**, then draw the new world at full opacity and the old at 20% opacity, dashed, in the same coordinates. One layout, two paintings.
149	
150	Each tile carries a diff state and that state drives its styling. In this stack there are four, all computed from the branch: `added` is solid with an accent ring; `killed` is ghosted, struck through, desaturated; **`downstream`** is drawn live — the claim your edit can reach, its number slot reading *"no engine yet"*; `untouched` is neutral, and it is the state the canvas can assert with confidence, because locality is a proven property and not a guess. The fifth state, `shifted` — `.61 → .18` with a directional chevron — arrives with the engine and needs no other change. **Never animate the diff as a crossfade** — `Space` toggles A ⇄ A′ as a hard switch, and the transition is scrubbable.
151	
152	**The delta rail** sits beside the canvas. With the engine it is the terminal changes, ranked, one line each — *"the Polymarket Brent contract · .61 → .18 ▼ · largest on Oct 9"* — in the order the engine gave them, with **two columns that are never folded into the rank**: `range_width` (how unsure we are of the number) and **`agreement`** (the share of the 2 000 versions of the map that moved the same way — the vocabulary's reserved word for a number computed from how far independent runs differed, never self-reported). They answer different questions and a trader weighs them separately, which is why they are columns. Before the engine lands, **both columns render as an absence with its reason**, like every other number slot in this stack. **This stack does not rank and does not compute**: until the engine lands, the rail lists the terminals your edit can reach, in map order, each with an absence and a reason where the number will go. A rail that invented an ordering would be inventing the one thing the rail exists to tell you.
153	
154	**UX-14, the overridden assertion.** A claim the user supposed true and that a later edit pushed back down never renders as plainly true. Its tile carries both states in order:
155	
156	> **Supposed · Oct 1 → Retracted · Oct 2 · by "a confirmed military strike on Iranian territory"**
157	
158	**While a claim is supposed, its tile shows the word where a likelihood would go** — *Supposed · Oct 1*, not `1.0` and not `.98`. The engine treats a supposition as a hard fact in every draw (stack 03a, Kent's decision of 2026-09-17), so there is no number to show, and inventing one would answer a question the user did not ask.
159	
160	Its series then carries three named states after that, and the tile and the time axis both read them: **supposed** → **withdrawn** (the supposition has been undermined and no opposing push has arrived yet — labelled *"withdrawn — no live push yet"*) → **pushed**. On the Hormuz branch that is Oct 1 supposed, Oct 2 to Oct 4 withdrawn at `.35`, Oct 5 onward pushed to about `.07`. The three-day gap between the badge's date and the day the number moves is the honest shape of the answer, and the interface must be able to say so rather than smoothing it away.
161	
162	Every part of that line is data on the world, not inference: the assignment gives *Supposed* and its date; the retraction gives the date, the arrow and the claim to name; `states` gives the three-state series. The **branch panel** lists that branch's edits in the order they were made, each with the badge its operation earns, so the surprising rule reads as a sequence rather than as a number that moved on its own.
163	
164	**The six buttons and badges, word for word from `spec/vocabulary.md`'s Interface words table** — copy them, do not paraphrase, and never show a code name:

167	|---|---|
168	| **Suppose this is true** (and **Suppose this is false**) | **Supposed · date** |
169	| **This happened** | **Happened · date** |
170	| **Add a claim** (hinted "…but this also happens") | **Added** |
171	| **Change this push** | **Retuned** |
172	| **Split this claim** | **Split** |
173	| **My own number** | none — the three-up belief chip is the badge |

179	**The keyboard map (UX-9).** `⌘K` command palette · `j`/`k` between siblings · `h`/`l` along wires between layers — arrow movement follows the *wires*, not screen space · `E` intervene · `B` branch · `Space` A ⇄ A′ · `?` the shortcuts sheet. We turn natural language — a thesis, strategy, hedge, or trading idea — into live execution across any market, venue, or asset class from prediction markets to commodities to tokens to private markets. 23	## Working agreements (interview, 2026-09-16)
24	
25	* **ADR-gated cadence.** An agent drafts the ADR and spec first; Kent accepts, rejects, or amends; only then is code written. Nothing is implemented against a `proposed` ADR. Decisions Kent has already taken are listed in `PRODUCT_REQUIREMENTS.md` §3 — do not re-litigate them.

30	* **ARCHITECTURE.md is living.** A pull request that changes a boundary, layer, data flow, or runtime dependency updates it in the same PR.
31	* **Research reports are inputs.** Where a report and an ADR disagree, the ADR wins; where an ADR and the PRD disagree, fix the drift in the same PR.

1	# PRODUCT_REQUIREMENTS.md — Katalyst
2	
3	> A causal-chain workbench for finance. You state a hypothesis; it builds an auditable graph of downstream events toward tradeable effects; you bend any link and watch the multiverse re-propagate; it ends in a thesis with a stop-loss you can name.
4	
5	**Status:** living document (L1.11: there is no shipping, only current state). **Owner:** Kent Gang. **Reader:** the Catalyst team (see §2). **Derived from:** `ASSIGNMENT.md`, `docs/initial-brainstorming.md`, `docs/research/*`, and the 2026-09-16 interview (§3). **Governed by:** `AGENTS.md`. **Companions:** `ARCHITECTURE.md` (how the system is shaped — the technical counterpart to this document), `docs/adr/` (numbered decision records — a journal), `spec/` (the detailed spec, organized as a book by idea).
6	
7	---
8	
9	## 1. What this is, in one screen
10	
11	**The hero use case, in one sentence.** You type an event you think will happen. Katalyst shows what it would cause, step by step, ending in trades — and lets you change any step to see how the trades change.
12	
13	**Input.** "The Strait of Hormuz is going to open next week." Optionally, a destination: "does that get me to Brent under $70?" Optionally, how likely *you* think it is — or "I don't know."
14	
15	**Output.** A map of cause and effect. Each box is a claim that can be checked by a date ("Brent closes under $70 by Nov 1, per ICE settlement"). Each box shows how likely it is as three numbers side by side: what the model thinks, what you think, and what the market is pricing. Each arrow states the mechanism, how strongly it pushes, and how long it takes. The map draws itself as the model reasons. It ends in things you can trade: a ticker, a contract, a commodity price.
16	
17	**The move.** Click any box and change it: "…but Iran is struck the next day." The original map is kept. A new version forks off. Only the boxes downstream of your change update. A faded overlay shows exactly what moved. Do this as often as you like and compare versions.
18	
19	**The finale.** A thesis card: what to buy or sell, when to enter, the one event that would prove the idea wrong (that is your stop-loss), the event that means take profit, and the rare disasters listed one by one rather than hidden inside an average. Exportable in a form a trading system can read.
20	
21	**Two doors, one map.** *Explore:* "Hormuz opens — what happens next, and what can I trade?" *Verify:* "Does Hormuz opening actually lead to cheaper oil — and where is that chain weakest?" Same map. Verify adds a destination, so the map grows toward it and grades every step. Explore is the first screen; Verify is one extra field, not a second product.
22	
23	**What it is not.** Not a chatbot with a diagram attached. Not an oracle: it lays out an argument, and every number can show why. Not a swarm of simulated agents. Not a place to execute trades.

They will not be impressed by another front door to an LLM; they will be impressed by a tool that turns a vague belief into something with a venue, a strike, an entry, a stop, and a falsifiability test — and does so honestly.
30	
31	The brief names three wants: **(a)** how black-swan events affect risk, **(b)** which events trigger stop-loss / take-profit, **(c)** whether a hypothesized event actually leads to the desired financial effect. 63	| **Hypothesis** | The user's root input: a proposition asserted as true (the `do` intervention below), carrying the user's own likelihood estimate |
64	| **Proposition** (node) | A *resolvable* claim: criteria, adjudicating source, resolve-by date. Kinds: `hypothesis`, `event`, `market` (instrument-bearing terminal) |
65	| **Link** (edge) | A causal claim from one proposition to another: `mode` (`trigger` — domino, fires once, decays; `sustain` — desk-holds-apple, effect retracts if cause is removed), `strength` (how much it shifts the odds of the next proposition; on a log-odds scale so several links add up), `lag`, `shape` (`impulse` \| `step` \| `ramp`), `half_life`, `rationale`, `sources`, `provenance` |
66	| **Provenance** | Where a number or link came from: `asserted` (model, no evidence) · `argued` (model + mechanism) · `documented` (cited sources) · `market_implied` (live price) · `historical` (event study) · `user` · `simulated` (probe) |
67	| **Belief** | A probability with an honest interval `{p, lo, hi}` and an owner: `model` \| `user` \| `market`. The three are never merged |
68	| **Graph** | Propositions and links with no loops (a directed acyclic graph). Loops are legal only through `reflexive` links — a market feeding back on the world — which must have a delay and unroll over time |
69	| **Intervention** | One of `do` (assert; cut parents; the button reads **Suppose this is true**), `observe` (learn; update parents too; the button reads **This happened**), `insert` (add a proposition + links), `retune` (change a link), `refine` (expand a proposition into sub-propositions that must marginalize back), `believe` (record the user's own belief on a proposition; shown beside the model's, not propagated in v1) |
70	| **Branch** | A named, ordered list of interventions over a base graph. A branch *is* a patch; branches compose by concatenation |
71	| **World** | A base graph with a branch applied and beliefs propagated. The base world is a branch with zero interventions |
72	| **Diff** | The structural and belief delta between two worlds: `unchanged` / `shifted` / `added` / `killed` per node, plus ranked terminal deltas |
73	| **Probe** (stretch) | Extra compute attached to one proposition: thousands of random simulations (Monte Carlo), a small probability model (Bayesian sub-net), or role-played experts hunting for gaps (persona red-team). Output re-enters the graph as a `simulated` belief |
74	| **Thesis** | The compiled trade: legs, entry, invalidation node, take-profit node, distribution, tails, caveats |

78	## 5. The hero flow
79	
80	```
81	 Launchpad ─▶ Hypothesis (+ optional target, + optional prior)
82	     │
83	     ▼
84	 Streaming generation ─▶ Graph grows layer by layer; wires draw in propagation order;
85	     │                   belief chips resolve last. Reasoning arrives as it is produced.
86	     ▼
87	 Inspect ─▶ any node/link: rationale, sources, base rate, model|user|market beliefs,
88	     │      "falsified if", conjunctive product of the path from the hypothesis
89	     ▼
90	 Intervene ─▶ "…but Iran is struck the next day" ⇒ branch forks, downstream re-propagates,
91	     │        ghost overlay + delta rail + one-line diff.  A ⇄ A′ on one key.
92	     ▼
93	 Drill down (stretch) ─▶ attach a probe where the thesis is most sensitive
94	     │
95	     ▼
96	 Thesis ─▶ card + live prices + export.  Invalidation node is derived, not typed.
97	```

101	## 6. Functional requirements
102	
103	Priority: **P0** — the hero flow does not exist without it. **P1** — the tool is not credible without it. **P2** — stretch; documented, designed for, not built first.
104	
105	### 6.1 Input and doors
106	- **FR-1 (P0)** Natural-language hypothesis input. Explore door (no target) or Verify door (target proposition B).
107	- **FR-2 (P0)** Ask for the user's own likelihood estimate at input as a range slider with an explicit "I don't know" state. Stored as a `user` belief on the hypothesis; never overwritten by the model.
108	- **FR-3 (P0)** Launchpad empty state seeds the four `ASSIGNMENT.md` examples as one-click cards. No illustration.
109	
110	### 6.2 Generation
111	- **FR-4 (P0)** The engine produces a graph in which every proposition is resolvable (INV-1) and every link carries mechanism, strength, lag, shape, provenance, and ≥1 source or an explicit `asserted` mark (INV-2).
112	- **FR-5 (P0)** Generation streams. Propositions and links arrive one at a time over server-sent events (a one-way stream from server to browser) and render as they arrive; layout reserves space so the graph grows without reflowing violently.
113	- **FR-6 (P0)** Every graph terminates in ≥1 `market` proposition, or in an explicit "not tradeable — because…" terminal (INV-9).
114	- **FR-7 (P0)** Verify door returns a graded path A→B or an explicit `no_path` verdict with the nearest reachable proposition. Never a fabricated bridge.
115	- **FR-8 (P1)** Ensemble: N independent generations reconciled into one graph; run-to-run disagreement surfaces as link *agreement* — a number computed from how far the independent runs differed, never a self-report by the model.
116	- **FR-9 (P1)** Adversarial critique pass before beliefs are final. **(P2)** Persona red-teams ("Lloyd's underwriter", "OPEC desk") that propose *missing* propositions and links — hypothesis diversity, not outcome simulation.
117	
118	### 6.3 Audit
119	- **FR-10 (P0)** Inspector (a panel, never a modal) for any proposition or link: rationale, sources, base rate and reference class, the three beliefs, "falsified if", resolution criteria.
120	- **FR-11 (P0)** Conjunctive honesty bar: for any path from the hypothesis to a selected proposition, show the product of link probabilities beside the narrative headline (INV-8).
121	- **FR-12 (P0)** Provenance is visibly encoded on every link and belief chip (INV-2, UX-6).
122	- **FR-13 (P0)** Replay: any world is reproducible from `(base graph id, branch, seed)`. Generation transcripts are stored with the graph.
123	
124	### 6.4 Multiverse
125	- **FR-14 (P0)** Interventions `do`, `observe`, `insert`, `retune`, `believe` on any proposition; committing one forks a branch implicitly; the base world is immutable (INV-5).
126	- **FR-15 (P0)** Re-propagation is local: only the intervened proposition and its descendants change; `sustain` links retract, `trigger` links do not (INV-4).
127	- **FR-16 (P0)** Diff: ghost overlay of A under A′ in a shared union layout; delta rail of terminal changes ranked by **the size of the move × the weakest backing on the path** from the edit to that terminal. Range width and **agreement** are shown beside as their own columns, never multiplied in — multiplying width in would sink exactly the claims FR-21 floats. A claim counts as **shifted** when it moved by .005 or more **and** moved in the same direction in at least 90% of versions of the map; that share is the agreement. One-line natural-language diff.
128	- **FR-17 (P1)** Compare ≥3 branches as small multiples; at most 4 branches visible, rest collapsed to a list; branches must be named.
129	- **FR-18 (P1)** `refine`: expand a proposition into sub-propositions; the children's combined likelihood must equal the parent's — they marginalize back (INV-10). This is the brainstorm's "search deeper lines".
130	
131	### 6.5 Sensitivity and drill-down
132	- **FR-19 (P1)** Sensitivity sweep: one-at-a-time flips of every proposition, ranking by adverse Δ on each terminal. Feeds FR-23 and FR-21.
133	- **FR-20 (P2)** Probes: attach a Monte Carlo, a Bayesian sub-net, or a persona red-team to one proposition; results re-enter as `simulated` beliefs with their own provenance and rationale.
134	- **FR-21 (P2)** "Where to spend modeling budget": rank propositions by **each stated range's share of the terminal's band** — how much of the width on the number you care about comes from not being sure of *this* claim — and say so in the UI. On the Hormuz example, 92% of the Brent claim's band is its own base rate; pin that down and the band goes from 29 points wide to 8.
135	
136	### 6.6 Risk
137	- **FR-22 (P0)** Tail strip: low-probability / high-magnitude propositions listed in a fixed strip with p, PnL, and a suggested hedge — never averaged into an expected value.
138	- **FR-23 (P0)** Invalidation derivation: the stop-loss is the proposition whose flip most damages the terminal, filtered to those that resolve *before* the terminal and are *publicly observable*. Take-profit is the symmetric case. Sensitive-but-unobservable propositions are listed as *unhedgeable*.
139	- **FR-24 (P1)** Payoff distribution from thousands of random simulations: the 10th / 50th / 90th-percentile outcomes, the average loss in the worst 5% of runs (CVaR₅), the largest peak-to-trough loss, and the chance of being wiped out. The actuarial "wiped out" case gets its own row.
140	
141	### 6.7 Thesis
142	- **FR-25 (P0)** Thesis card: hypothesis, horizon, legs (instrument, direction, size, driving proposition, model p, market p, edge), entry, invalidation, take-profit, distribution (P1), tails, caveats (weakest links, unhedgeable sensitivities, crowding).
143	- **FR-26 (P1)** Live read-only prices: Polymarket first, FRED second, Kalshi third. Shown beside model and user beliefs as the `market` belief. Cross-venue disagreement is surfaced, not averaged. FRED data renders the required attribution line ("This product uses the FRED® API but is not endorsed or certified by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis").
144	- **FR-27 (P1)** Strategy export: a declarative JSON document (schema in `spec/thesis/`) with legs, conditions, and the graph references that justify each — the shape a downstream trading agent could ingest.
145	
146	### 6.8 Grounding
147	- **FR-28 (P1)** Evidence retrieval at generation time (server-side web search); sources attach to links with direction and weight.
148	- **FR-29 (P2)** Historical-analog panel: for a link, past instances and how prices moved around them, with an uncertainty band (an event study).
149	- **FR-30 (P2)** Pastcast self-test: run a chain on a resolved 2024–25 event with a date-frozen corpus and show the Brier score (the standard accuracy score for probability forecasts; lower is better), including when it is bad.
150	
151	### 6.9 Persistence and sharing
152	- **FR-31 (P0)** Sessions (graph + branches + transcripts) persist to a single SQLite file (a one-file database, no server) and are addressable by URL. No accounts in v1.

156	## 7. UI/UX requirements — the *Workbench*
157	
158	The direction is D3. The research's "Instrument" craft rules (typography, color, motion) still apply; the *shell* is a workbench, not a terminal.
159	
160	- **UX-1 Node tiles are rich.** A proposition renders as a card with: claim, kind silhouette, belief chips (model | user | market) as a three-up, a density sparkline when quantitative, evidence clippings (source favicon + one line), and the resolve-by date. Fixed width, clamped height, 8px grid. Detail lives in the Inspector, not the tile.
161	- **UX-2 Ports and wires are typed.** Propositions have input and output ports; a link is a wire whose *stroke* encodes signal shape (impulse: dot-dash; step: solid; ramp: gradient) and whose *weight* encodes |strength|; `sustain` wires are double-stroked; `reflexive` wires loop with a visible lag chip. The midpoint chip shows the conditional probability in the Metaculus arrow-and-bar idiom.
162	- **UX-3 World state is visible.** A strip shows the terminal instruments as gauges (Brent, a basket, a contract) with their model | user | market readings, re-ticking on intervention. Time is a scrubbable axis; lags are real distances.
163	- **UX-4 Level of detail by zoom.** Far: worlds and their terminal deltas. Mid: wiring and belief chips. Near: the full tile with evidence. Text never shrinks below 11px; the tile changes representation instead.
164	- **UX-5 Organizability.** Users can pin, group, and annotate tiles (mood-board affordance); automatic layered layout (the ELK library, left→right) is the default and re-layout preserves the focused tile's screen position. Dragging is either fully supported or absent — never half.
165	- **UX-6 Color is law.** Probability → luminance/opacity. Direction of financial effect → blue ▲ / amber ▼, always with glyph and sign, never red/green. Branch identity → a small ordered palette on lanes and chips only. Tail risk → hatch texture, not hue. Provenance → stroke style (`asserted` dashed). No information in hue alone (INV-12).
166	- **UX-7 Motion budget.** Three animations: propagation wave (wires draw in causal order, ~200ms staggered), branch creation, belief number-roll. Everything else ≤120ms opacity. `prefers-reduced-motion` keeps ordering and drops tweening.
167	- **UX-8 Streaming is the loading state.** No spinner. Skeleton tiles appear at their layer, claims stream in, wires draw, chips resolve last. Reasoning arrives as it is produced.
168	- **UX-9 Keyboard first.** `⌘K` palette; `j/k` siblings; `h/l` layers along wires; `E` intervene; `B` branch; `Space` A⇄A′; `?` sheet. Focus is always visible.
169	- **UX-10 No modals.** One persistent Inspector; confirmations are undoable toasts.
170	- **UX-11 Typography.** One UI face and one tabular-figures mono for every number; three sizes, three weights; hierarchy by color and spacing. Not the component library's defaults.
171	- **UX-12 Themes and access.** Dark-first, light verified, semantic tokens. All text and glyphs ≥4.5:1. The graph also exists as an outline (`role="tree"`) with a screen-reader announcement (`aria-live`) when a branch re-propagates.
172	- **UX-13 Empty and edge states.** Launchpad (FR-3); `no_path` verdict as a first-class card; "not tradeable — because…" terminal as a first-class card.
173	- **UX-14 An overridden assertion says so.** A claim the user supposed true, and that a later edit in the same branch has pushed back down, never renders as plainly true. Its tile carries both states in order — *Supposed · Oct 1 → Retracted · Oct 2 by "confirmed strike on Iranian territory"* — naming the edit responsible, and the branch panel lists that branch's edits in the order they were made. This is what makes the rule that a later `insert` outranks an earlier assertion readable on screen rather than surprising.

177	## 8. Non-functional requirements
178	
179	- **NFR-1 Honesty.** Beliefs render at two significant figures with their interval (`.35 (.2–.5)`), never `.347`. Every number is one click from rationale, sources, base rate.
180	- **NFR-2 Determinism.** Propagation is pure and seeded; the same `(graph, branch, seed)` yields byte-identical worlds.
181	- **NFR-3 Tests.** The core graph code is property-tested (the Hypothesis library generates thousands of random graphs and shrinks any failure to a minimal example) against the invariants in §9; the model boundary is tested with recorded API responses ("cassettes") committed to the repo; evals run out-of-band on the four assignment examples. CI is green with no API key (INV-13).
182	- **NFR-4 Docker.** `docker compose up` yields a working app; `docker compose watch` gives hot reload for both halves; a production-ish compose builds slim images with healthchecks. No database service in v1.
183	- **NFR-5 Legibility.** Every architectural decision is a numbered decision record; every feature with invariants has a spec; every PR names the invariant it satisfies; conventional commits with `spec:` and `adr:` types.
184	- **NFR-6 Cost visibility.** Each generation records model, tokens, cache hits, and dollars; shown in the Inspector's transcript view.
185	- **NFR-7 Performance.** 60 tiles render and re-layout in <100ms on a laptop; streaming first-paint within 1s of the first token.
186	- **NFR-8 Secrets.** One `.env.example`; keys read once via settings; a secret scanner (`gitleaks`) runs before every commit; recorded API responses are scrubbed of keys.

190	## 9. Invariants
191	
192	Phrased as checkable statements. Each names the spec that owns it; specs name the property test. If an invariant cannot name a test strategy, it is a wish and belongs in §6.
193	
194	| ID | Invariant | Owner |
195	|----|-----------|-------|
196	| INV-1 | **Checkable.** Every proposition has resolution criteria, a named adjudicating source, and a resolve-by date | `spec/graph/` |
197	| INV-2 | **Says why.** Every link has a rationale and a provenance; a link that claims evidence (documented, historical, or market-implied) carries at least one source. Every belief has an owner | `spec/graph/` |
198	| INV-3 | **Assert is not observe.** Asserting a proposition (`do`) changes nothing upstream of it; observing it (`observe`) may. Two operations, two verbs in the interface | `spec/multiverse/` |
199	| INV-4 | **Locality.** An intervention changes only what is still connected to its subject in the graph the edit leaves behind; every other proposition is byte-identical between the base and the branch. Operational form: the affected-set table in `spec/multiverse/interventions.md`, which names the set for each of the six operations | `spec/multiverse/` |
200	| INV-5 | **Branches are patches.** The base graph is never modified. A branch is an ordered list of interventions. Applying an empty branch changes nothing; applying two branches in sequence equals applying their concatenation. Every world replays exactly from (base, branch, seed) | `spec/multiverse/` |
201	| INV-6 | **No loops.** Ignoring *reflexive* links (a market feeding back on the world), the graph has no cycles; every reflexive link carries a delay greater than zero | `spec/graph/` |
202	| INV-7 | **Honest numbers.** Every belief satisfies 0 ≤ low ≤ p ≤ high ≤ 1 after any sequence of interventions, and is rendered at two significant figures with its range | `spec/graph/`, `spec/workbench/` |
203	| INV-8 | **Chains multiply.** Any displayed path shows the product of its link probabilities beside the narrative headline | `spec/workbench/` |
204	| INV-9 | **Ends in a trade.** Every graph has at least one tradeable terminal, or an explicit "not tradeable — because…" terminal | `spec/graph/` |
205	| INV-10 | **Refinement adds up.** After a proposition is split into finer sub-propositions, their combined likelihood equals the original's within a small tolerance | `spec/multiverse/` |
206	| INV-11 | **Three voices.** Model, user, and market beliefs are stored and rendered separately; no code path averages them | `spec/graph/`, `spec/workbench/` |
207	| INV-12 | **Not by color alone.** Every direction has a glyph, every tail a texture, every provenance a stroke style | `spec/workbench/` |
208	| INV-13 | **Keyless CI.** Continuous integration runs with no model API key; the model boundary is exercised only through recorded responses | `spec/generation/` |
209	| INV-14 | **A stop you can see.** The invalidation proposition resolves before its terminal and is publicly observable; otherwise it is listed as unhedgeable, never used as a stop | `spec/thesis/` |

213	## 10. Anti-patterns
214	
215	Phrased as *do not X, because Y; do Z instead.*
216	
217	1. Do not let the LLM assign IDs or own graph validity — it collides across branches and invents cycles. Mint IDs server-side; validate in the domain layer; reject, don't repair silently.
218	2. Do not re-prompt for the whole graph after an edit — it breaks locality (INV-4) and auditability. Re-propagate mathematically; re-prompt only for `insert` on the affected subtree.
219	3. Do not conflate conditioning with intervention — "P(oil ↓ | Hormuz open)" is correlational. Offer `do` and `observe` as separate verbs and say which one the user is doing.
220	4. Do not average model, user, and market beliefs into one number — the product's value is the gap between them (INV-11).
221	5. Do not render `.347` — precision beyond two significant figures on an elicited number is a lie (NFR-1).
222	6. Do not headline an expected value — tails get their own rows (FR-22). EV hides the wipe-out.
223	7. Do not simulate an agent society to produce outcomes — unvalidated and the audience pattern-matches it as theater. Use personas only to propose missing structure (FR-9).
224	8. Do not use Markov steady states or chaotic dynamics as the engine — these events are one-shot and non-ergodic. Time-unroll lagged links instead.
225	9. Do not ship a force-directed hairball, a spinner-then-dump, a modal, or the component library's default look — each is a D5 veto condition.
226	10. Do not let a chain end in prose — every terminal is an instrument or an explicit "not tradeable" (INV-9).
227	11. Do not type the stop-loss by hand — derive it from sensitivity (FR-23) and show the derivation.
228	12. Do not put a database, auth, or multi-tenancy in v1 — three failure modes and zero value to the reader. SQLite file on a volume.
229	13. Do not implement against a `proposed` decision record (D9).

41	**What runs, and what is drawn ahead.** The browser app and the Python server both start, and `api/` answers three things for real: whether the server is up, what it calls itself, and the stored worked example. `domain/` holds the rules and nothing else. `[planned]` Four parts of the drawing have no code behind them. There is no event stream — every route today is an ordinary request and its answer. `engine/` holds identifier minting alone; nothing has ever called Anthropic's API. `grounding/` is an empty package; nothing has ever called Polymarket or FRED. There is no storage: no database file, no volume declared in either compose file, nothing kept between requests. Inside the browser box only a status screen exists; the canvas, the inspector, the world-state strip and the thesis dock are drawn because they are decided, not because they are written.

43	Two halves, one contract: the backend publishes an OpenAPI description (a machine-readable list of every route and data shape); the frontend's TypeScript types are generated from it and committed, and continuous integration fails if regeneration would change them.
